 8                      III. CLASS COST OF SERVICE STUDY

 9   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF COST OF SERVICE ANALYSIS?

10   A.   A cost of service analysis is conducted to assist in determining appropriate rates for

11        each customer class. It involves the assignment of revenues, expenses, and rate

12        base to each customer class and includes the following steps:

13        •   Functionalization: Separating the utility’s costs in accordance with the various

14            functions of its system (e.g., generation (or production), transmission, and

15            distribution);

16        •   Classification: Classifying the utility’s costs with respect to the manner in

17            which they are incurred by customers (e.g., customer-related costs, demand-

18            related costs, and energy-related costs); and




                                                8
                                        Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                  Direct Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1        •   Allocation: Allocating responsibility for the utility’s costs to the various

 2            customer classes based on principles of cost causation.

 3   Q.   WHAT IS THE ROLE OF THE COST OF SERVICE ANALYSIS IN

 4        SETTING RATES?

 5   A.   Each of the three steps above has an important role in the ratemaking process. Cost

 6        functionalization guides classification and the allocation method based on the

 7        utility function served.

 8               The classification of costs informs the selection of allocation methods (i.e.,

 9        demand, energy, or customer-based). The classification of costs is also critical to

10        the rate design process (i.e., in determining the proper customer charge, demand

11        charge, and energy charge for each rate schedule).

12               Finally, the allocation of costs to customer classes guides the revenue

13        allocation across customer classes, commonly referred to as “rate spread.” In

14        determining rate spread, it is important to align rates with cost causation to the

15        greatest extent practicable. Properly aligning rates with the costs caused by each

16        customer class is essential for ensuring fairness, as it minimizes cross subsidies

17        among customers. It also sends proper price signals, which improves efficiency in

18        resource utilization.

 1   Q.       HOW DOES SPS ALLOCATE PRODUCTION AND TRANSMISSION

 2            PLANT IN ITS EMBEDDED CCOSS?

 3   A.       SPS proposes to use an embedded CCOSS that allocates demand and energy

 4            functions based upon customer class kW and kWh from the Future Test Year

 5            (“FTY”) forecast, adjusted for line losses.1 SPS witness Taylor J. Hurt explains

 6            that SPS proposes to allocate production-related plant, except the Hale and

 7            Sagamore wind generation facilities, using the AED-4CP method with the line-loss

 8            adjusted energy usage and 4CP demands for the four peak months of June through

 9            September.2 SPS also proposes to allocate the majority transmission-related plant

10            using the AED-4CP method.3

11   Q.       PLEASE DESCRIBE THE AED-4CP ALLOCATION METHOD.

12   A.       The AED-4CP allocation method is a variant of the Average and Excess (“AED”)

13            method, which is described in detail in the Electric Utility Cost Allocation Manual

14            published by the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners

15            (“NARUC Manual”) in its section entitled “Energy Weighting Methods.” As stated

16            in the NARUC Manual, the AED method “effectively uses an average demand, or

17            total energy allocator, to allocate the portion of the utility’s generating capacity that

 1              would be needed if all customers used energy at a constant 100 percent load

 2              factor.”4 This portion of the cost is weighted by the system load factor. The cost

 3              of capacity above average demand is then allocated in proportion to each class’s

 4              excess demand, where excess demand, per the AED-4CP variant, is measured as

 5              the difference between each class’s 4CP demand and its average demand. This

 6              portion of the cost is weighted by 1 minus the system load factor. This allocation

 7              of excess demand ensures that the incremental amount of production plant that is

 8              required to meet loads that are above average demand is assigned to the users who

 9              create the need for the additional capacity.

 1   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY THE FACT THAT SPS HAS ALREADY

 2        ALLOCATED A SIGNIFICANT NUMBER OF PTCS FROM THE HALE

13        plant occurs over a much longer time period. This creates a mismatch between the

14        timing of the cost recovery for these facilities and the PTC benefits. Hale began

15        commercial operations in 2019 while Sagamore began operating in 2020. Since a

16        significant number of PTCs have already been allocated based on energy, it would

 1   Q.   WHAT       IS     YOUR       RECOMMENDATION               REGARDING           THE

 2        APPROPRIATE ALLOCATION OF PRODUCTION PLANT?

 3   A.   If the Hale and Sagamore wind plants are carved out and allocated on a separate

 4        basis from the rest of SPS’s production plant, then the load served with generation

 5        from the Hale and Sagamore wind plants should also be excluded from the AED-

 6        4CP calculations. Specifically, the expected coincident peak contribution of the

 7        Hale and Sagamore wind plants as well as the annual expected energy from the

 8        facilities should be excluded from the calculation of system load factor used to

 9        weight the energy component in the AED-4CP. It would not be appropriate or

10        consistent to include the load served by generation from these facilities within the

11        AED-4CP calculations if the plant is allocated using a different method.

12   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY IT WOULD BE INCONSISTENT TO INCLUDE

13        THE LOAD SERVED BY THE HALE AND SAGAMORE GENERATION

14        IN THE AED-4CP CALCULATIONS IF THE COSTS OF THOSE WIND

15        PLANTS ARE CARVED OUT?

16   A.   The AED-4CP method is predicated on using total system attributes (e.g., load

17        factor and peak demands) to allocate the entire portfolio of production assets used

18        to serve the overall system. If the wind plant is segregated from the rest of the

19        production plant for the purpose of class cost allocation, then the use of the AED-

 1   4CP method necessarily would be limited to allocating the fixed cost of all other

 2   production plant. As the allocation of production plant is a function of the load

 3   served by that plant, the amount of retail load served by Hale and Sagamore must

 4   be removed from the AED-4CP analysis if the wind plant is allocated separately

 5   from all other plant. Otherwise, the cost allocation parameters used in allocating

 6   the non-wind plant would be distorted by the inclusion of Hale and Sagamore

 7   production data and the corresponding load being served.
